newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends lower in Europe, hit by German data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends lower in Europe, hit by German data.

text.p: The dollar closed lower in European trading as the mark and the yen gained some ground but it managed to hold its head above key support levels.

Dealers said the dollar was dragged down by a combination of negative factors, such as stong German data, a sterling slide, a rise in Japan's call rate and a comment from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer for an end to the dollar/mark appreciation.

"The mark-friendly German data was one of the factors that weighed on the dollar but the downmove should be seen as part of a consolidation rather than pronounced weakness," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The Ifo West German business climate index rose to 93.3 in January from December's 90.9. German January M3 money supply grew 8.6 percent compared to the fourth quarter 1995 of and 11.7 percent versus fourth-quarter 1996.

"I doubt the latest Ifo data will change the market's perception about the German economy but it was a little shaft of light which aided the mark," said Meggyesi. "But the market will remain sceptical of the German economy as long as the jobless figures don't improve."
Dollar/mark was at 1.6878/83 at 1622 GMT from 1.6970/75 late here on Wednesday. Dollar/yen was at 122.88/98 from 124.30/35.

Sonia Gibbs, strategist at Nomura, said both sets of German data were well above expectations. "It shows that we do have a fairly strong cyclical recovery and we are seeing the effect of the weaker mark," said Gibbs.

The dollar was also hit by a fresh call from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer for an end to the dollar/mark appreciation. He said the recent rise was a correction, "but we are not interested in a correction process that would go beyond tolerable limits".
Tietmeyer also said a German rate cut was not likely in the short term.
The mark surged against the Norwegian crown after Norway's central bank said it would resume foreign currency purchases to the equivalent of three billion crowns a month in 1997.

Oil-rich Norway expects to have a budget surplus of 55.4 billion crowns in 1997, which will be placed in the government Petroleum Fund. Norges Bank is charged with converting the money into foreign currency and investing overseas.

"The purchases must be seen against a background of Norges Bank's role as a manager of the Petroleum Fund and, as such, the purchases are not undertaken as exchange market interventions," the central bank said in a statement.

In January, Norges Bank said it would no longer intervene to a substantial extent in the foreign exchange market over a period. This followed a spate of heavy crown selling by the central bank aimed at curbing the currency's strength.
The crown slumped to a low of 4.0340 on the annoucement, its lowest since January 24 and down from around 3.9738 at the open.
"The market took this as a bearish signal for the crown," said Meggyesi at DMG. "The decision to pull out of the market back in January was what allowed the crown to appreciate."
But analysts also noted the crown sell-off might have been an overreaction as the annoucement was not a reversal of policy.

The yen, meanwhile, got support from a newspaper report saying the Japanese government was planning to use public money to buy real estate from ailing mortgage and financial companies. This boosted Japanese stocks and hit bonds amid talk that such a plan would lessen the need to keep interest rates low.

Dealers also noted the Japanese call rate had touched 0.53 percent, edging above the 0.50 percent discount rate. That suggested to some that Japan is getting more serious about halting the yen's slide.

Sterling got hit by news that the Confederation of British Industry had cut its growth forecast, citing the pound's strength. The CBI cut its 1997 GDP forecast to 2.8 percent from 3.1 percent and its inflation forecast to 2.2 percent from 2.5 percent.
Sterling dropped from near 2.75 marks below 2.17 marks on the news before recovering to 2.7153/58 in late trade.

The Italian lira, undermined by EMU worries in the last few days, returned to its central parity of 990 per mark as dealers took profits on mark positions ahead of the release of Italian preliminary inflation data for February.
